intro.uz: Bu matn 35 yoshida buxgalterlikdan novvoylikka oʻtgan ayol haqida. Oʻqishdan oldin oʻylab koʻring: kattaroq yoshda kasbni oʻzgartirish oson deb oʻylaysizmi?

paragraphs.en: For twelve years, Shahlo Karimova worked as an accountant in a large office in Namangan. She had a good salary, a comfortable chair and a computer full of numbers. Her family was proud of her stable job. But every evening, when she came home, she did the one thing that really made her happy: she baked. Cakes, bread, biscuits with walnuts: her kitchen always smelled of something warm.

For a long time, baking was only a hobby. Friends and neighbours often ordered cakes for birthdays, and Shahlo never asked them to pay much. Then, in the year she turned thirty-five, her company was reorganised and her department was closed. She was offered a similar job in another city, but it would have meant leaving her children with her parents for most of the week.

Shahlo remembers that this was the moment when she had to make a decision. Her husband encouraged her to try baking professionally, but her mother was less sure. She told Shahlo that a bakery was a risky business and that an accountant should know this better than anyone. Shahlo agreed that it was risky. However, she also knew that if she did not try, she would always wonder what might have happened.

She started small. She rented a tiny room near a busy market, bought a second-hand oven and got up at four every morning to bake. Her experience as an accountant turned out to be very useful: she knew exactly how much each loaf cost to make, and she kept careful records of every sale. In the first six months, she earned less than she had earned in the office. More than once, she wanted to give up.

Today, three years later, Shahlo's bakery employs five people, and customers queue outside on Friday mornings for her walnut bread. She works longer hours than before, but she says that she is much happier. When young people ask her for advice, she tells them that it is never too late to change direction. They do not have to throw away their old skills, she explains. They just have to find a new place to use them.
